'''Elizabeth L. Brainerd''' (born 1963) is an American biologist who has contributed to our understanding of the [[evolution]] of breathing<ref>{{Citation|chapter=Major Transformations in Vertebrate Breathing Mechanisms|pages=47–62|publisher=University of Chicago Press|isbn=9780226268255|doi=10.7208/chicago/9780226268392.003.0003|title=Great Transformations in Vertebrate Evolution|year=2015}}</ref> and the [[biomechanics]] of [[vertebrate]]s. She is one of the inventors of XROMM (X-ray Reconstruction of Moving Morphology),<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Brainerd|first1=Elizabeth L.|last2=Baier|first2=David B.|last3=Gatesy|first3=Stephen M.|last4=Hedrick|first4=Tyson L.|last5=Metzger|first5=Keith A.|last6=Gilbert|first6=Susannah L.|last7=Crisco|first7=Joseph J.|date=2010|title=X-ray reconstruction of moving morphology (XROMM): precision, accuracy and applications in comparative biomechanics research|journal=Journal of Experimental Zoology Part A: Ecological Genetics and Physiology|volume=9999A|issue=5|pages=262–79|doi=10.1002/jez.589|pmid=20095029|bibcode=2010JEZA..313..262B |issn=1932-5223}}</ref> a technique for making 3D movies of internal structure that combines [[CT scan]]ning with biplanar [[x-ray]] movies. She is one of the authors of ''Great Transformations in Vertebrate Evolution''.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Great transformations in vertebrate evolution|others=Dial, Kenneth Paul; Shubin, Neil; Brainerd, Elizabeth L.|date=20 July 2015 |isbn=9780226268118|location=Chicago|oclc=894026103}}</ref>

Brainerd is the Robert P. Brown Professor of Biology professor of Biology<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://today.brown.edu/announcements/127013|title=Today@Brown|website=today.brown.edu|access-date=2020-02-22}}</ref> and of Medical Science in the Ecology and Evolutionary Biology Department at [[Brown University]], Providence, Rhode Island.

== Early life and education ==
She was born in 1963 to Lyman and Susan Brainerd. She attended the [[The Putney School|Putney School]] in Vermont, then [[Harvard University]], where in 1985 she graduated with an AB. She joined the lab of Karel F. Liem at Harvard where she earned a Ph.D. in 1991.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.qstormlegacy.org/beth-brainerd-profile/|title=Beth Brainerd – Profile {{!}} Qstorm|language=en-US|access-date=2019-11-10}}</ref> She then moved to Tom McMahon's lab for her post doctoral work as a [[Harvard Society of Fellows|Junior Fellow]] in the Harvard Society of Fellows (1990–1993).<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://socfell.fas.harvard.edu/listed-term-0|title=Listed by Term|website=socfell.fas.harvard.edu|language=en|access-date=2019-11-10}}</ref>

== Academic career ==
In graduate school Brainerd's mentors included Indonesian born ichthyologist Karel F. Liem and the paleontologists [[Farish Jenkins]] and [[Alfred W. Crompton|Alfred (Fuzz) Crompton]]. Brainerd's first academic appointment was at the [[University of Massachusetts Amherst|University of Massachusetts – Amherst]] (1994–2006). She then moved to Brown University where she runs the Functional Morphology and Biomechanics lab and teaches human gross anatomy in the medical school. She has been the president of the International Society of Vertebrate Morphologists<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.isvm.info/executive_committee.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150202044434/http://www.isvm.info/executive_committee.html|url-status=usurped|archive-date=February 2, 2015|title=ISVM|website=www.isvm.info|access-date=2019-11-11}}</ref> and the [[Society for Integrative and Comparative Biology]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://sicb.org/|title=Society for Integrative and Comparative Biology|website=sicb.org|language=en|access-date=2019-11-11}}</ref>

=== Honors ===
Brainerd is a Fellow of the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.aaas.org/fellows/listing|title=Elected Fellows|website=American Association for the Advancement of Science|language=en|access-date=2019-11-10}}</ref> She has won the Dean's Award for Excellence in Graduate Mentoring (2015)<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://vivo.brown.edu/display/ebrainer|title=Brainerd, Elizabeth|website=vivo.brown.edu|access-date=2019-11-09}}</ref> and in 2018 was selected as a Gilliam Fellowship Mentor by the [[Howard Hughes Medical Institute]]. In 2020 she was named the Robert P. Brown Professor of Biology<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://today.brown.edu/announcements/127013|title=Today@Brown|website=today.brown.edu|access-date=2020-02-22}}</ref> and became a fellow of the American Association for Anatomy.<ref>{{Cite web |title=List of Fellows: American Association for Anatomy |url=https://www.anatomy.org/ANATOMY/ANATOMY/Awards-Programs/Award-Recipients-Lists/List-of-AAA-Fellows.aspx}}</ref> In 2021 she won the Joseph S. Nelson Lifetime Achievement Award in Ichthyology.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Joseph S. Nelson Lifetime Achievement Award in Ichthyology: Award Announcement |url=https://www.asih.org/awards/nelson-award}}</ref> In 2023 she gave the Bidder Prize Lecture for the [[Society for Experimental Biology]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Bidder Lecture Award |url=https://www.sebiology.org/grants/award-listing/seb-plenary-lecture-award/bidder-lecture-award.html}}</ref>

== Selected works ==
{{Scholia|author}}
She has published more than 100 peer reviewed publications. Highlights include the realization that breathing is two separate events, inhalation and exhalation;<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Brainerd|first=E. L.|date=December 1999|title=New perspectives on the evolution of lung ventilation mechanisms in vertebrates|journal=Experimental Biology Online|volume=4|issue=2|pages=1–28|doi=10.1007/s00898-999-0002-1|bibcode=1999EvBO....4b...1B |issn=1430-3418}}</ref> how lizards (and dinosaurs) run and breathe at the same time;<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.umass.edu/newsoffice/article/research-umass-amherst-biologist-suggests-lizards-offer-evolutionary-freeze-frame|title=Research by UMass Amherst Biologist Suggests that Lizards Offer Evolutionary Freeze-Frame|website=Office of News & Media Relations {{!}} UMass Amherst|language=en|access-date=2019-11-10}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Owerkowicz|first=T.|s2cid=19857128|date=1999-06-04|title=Contribution of Gular Pumping to Lung Ventilation in Monitor Lizards|journal=Science|volume=284|issue=5420|pages=1661–1663|doi=10.1126/science.284.5420.1661|pmid=10356394|issn=0036-8075|bibcode=1999Sci...284.1661O}}</ref> The invention of the [https://jeb.biologists.org/content/jexbio/176/1/11.full.pdf 'Ram-Suction index' for studying prey capture]; and the contribution of vertebral number and joint flexibility of [[Mauthner cell|C-starts]] in fishes.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Brainerd|first1=Elizabeth L.|last2=Patek|first2=Sheila N.|date=1998-12-30|title=Vertebral Column Morphology, C-Start Curvature, and the Evolution of Mechanical Defenses in Tetraodontiform Fishes|journal=Copeia|volume=1998|issue=4|pages=971|doi=10.2307/1447344|issn=0045-8511|jstor=1447344}}</ref> She described the inflation mechanism of puffer fish<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Brainerd|first=Elizabeth L.|date=June 1994|title=Pufferfish inflation: Functional morphology of postcranial structures inDiodon holocanthus (Tetraodontiformes)|journal=Journal of Morphology|volume=220|issue=3|pages=243–261|doi=10.1002/jmor.1052200304|pmid=29865387|bibcode=1994JMorp.220..243B |issn=0362-2525}}</ref> and the x-ray movies she generated were used by [[Pixar]] in animating the character Bloat in [[Finding Nemo]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.qstormlegacy.org/beth-brainerd-profile/|title=Beth Brainerd – Profile {{!}} Qstorm|access-date=2019-11-09}}</ref>
